en: Words denoting action have the sense of being (bhāva) as their meaning; from them, the action is to be understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.1)
First, he establishes the connection between the two definitions. In that regard, it was stated that the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) was completed in the first chapter;
however, that is incorrect.
Why is this?
For indeed, in the first chapter, the author of the Sūtras has not described at all the essential nature of the means of valid cognition and so forth by means of a definition. (1)
A definition is said to be that by which the essential nature of a thing is determined as having an excluded form from those things distinct from it.
And such a definition has not been stated for [the categories] beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For, to begin with, inference (*anumāna*) and the others have not even been set forth in the aphorisms.
It has been explained that even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is presented as not being a means of knowledge (*animitta*) with respect to *dharma*, and not as its object of definition (*lakṣya*);
nor has any verbal testimony (*śabda*) that constitutes a valid means of knowledge for *dharma* been defined, since it is precisely this [verbal testimony] that is to be defined in this very section.
Furthermore, although the author of the commentary has presented definitions for all [categories], it is not proper to conclude that these constitute the subject matter of the chapter;
for there is no conclusion drawn regarding the subject matter of the chapter as stated in the sūtras.
Moreover, how could the sūtras be exhausted by a subject matter entirely distinct from the meaning of the definitions taken as a whole?
Moreover,
even that group of six which was mentioned by the author of the *Vṛtti* as being preceded by perception is not within the scope of the definition, precisely because it is not to be examined. (2)
For those [terms] whose meanings are well-known in the world have been stated as being beyond critical examination; they do not deserve to be included as subjects of the first chapter.
Therefore, having considered what occurred in the first chapter, this commentary should be understood accordingly.

In this regard, the definition of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is based upon the characteristic of Vedic injunction (codanā); furthermore, the determination of the true nature of injunctions and so forth is established by means of valid cognition alone. (3)
For the first quarter [of the first chapter] in its entirety is an auxiliary to the *codanālakṣaṇa* sūtra;
and therein, it was stated that dharma has the injunction (*codanā*) as its defining characteristic.

Therefore, because the word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is used in association with a meaning already determined, the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) must be etymologically derived as "that by which something is cognized" (*pramīyate*), and thus explained solely with reference to dharma.

Even though this treatise refers to the mere object of cognition (*prameya*), since *dharma* was introduced as the subject to be investigated (*jijñāsya*), it is that very thing which is understood here.
Alternatively, the instrument itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and its definition alone has been stated.

And although that [definition] has not been stated for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, it is considered to have been stated by this much alone: that the definition of the means of valid cognition regarding *dharma* is "being an injunction" (*codanātva*).
Nor is it necessary that something possesses the status of a definition only when it is defined in its entirety;
for since specific forms are infinite, there is an absence of a universal definition [for them].

This follows from the context of the preceding discussion; moreover, even the specific distinction has already been stated in the *Autpattikasūtra*, by which the particularity of the tradition (*āgama*) is understood.

Alternatively, this is the conclusion: the definition—that is, the cause of its authoritative status—has been stated for the means of knowledge consisting of *codanā* which was introduced [at the beginning].

Likewise, although it was not explicitly stated that "this is the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), this is the nature of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and this is the nature of a mantra," nevertheless, because their utility with respect to *dharma* has been declared, their true essence has been determined.
However, their specific forms were not pointed out due to the lack of an appropriate occasion.
The fact that knowledge is rooted in Śruti is the essential principle for the authority of Smṛti.

A name possesses authority because it is included within an injunction (codanā). In the determination of a doubtful meaning, both the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) and contextual capacity (sāmarthya) possess authority. Thus, they describe this entire chapter as the "Definition of Authority" (pramāṇalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, this must not be forgotten.
For one who has not forgotten [the Buddha's] authority will tolerate the demonstration of distinctions and so forth being made, lest it be rendered useless due to a lack of distinction;
otherwise, he would even object that such a demonstration is indeed purposeless.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the consideration of what is primary (*pradhāna*) and what is secondary (*apradhāna*) is the subject matter of the third and fourth [chapters], so why is it introduced here?
Some say:

"Because here there is an investigation into the primary and secondary status of both substances (*dravya*) and actions (*karman*), whereas in the subsequent [chapter] there is an investigation into the primary and secondary status of actions alone; thus, there is no tautology."
That is incorrect, because in the rule "in the case of substances, qualities, and preparations" (dravyaguṇasaṃskāreṣu), everything is already denoted; therefore,
it should be stated as follows:
In this context, the distinction [between the means of knowledge] is established in reality through their defining characteristics, such as the difference in verbal expression and so forth;
following that, even the distinction of the "unprecedented" (apūrva) is primary for the sake of establishing that [distinction].
First, the differentiation of action (*karmabheda*) is the general definition;
non-differentiation is its exception.
However, the differentiation and non-differentiation of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) follow as a consequence of those.

In that context, once the contingency of distinct *apūrva*s has arisen for each distinct ritual action (*karman*), the third established discussion concerning primary and secondary actions will now be undertaken as an exception (*apavāda*).

Even though acts such as threshing (*avahanana*) are distinct from one another based on differences in verbal expression and other criteria, no separate *apūrva* produced by an action arises, because these acts terminate in visible purposes required by the ritual action.
As for the *apūrva* resulting from restrictive rules (*niyama*), it is not caused by the [physical] action itself and is therefore not designated by it.

Therefore, wherever actions possess primacy with respect to substances and so forth, it is precisely there that the distinction of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is established based on the distinction of those [actions]. To distinguish this, the definition of what is subordinate (*guṇa*) and what is primary (*pradhāna*) will be stated; furthermore, two sections (*adhikaraṇa*) will be introduced for the purpose of providing exceptions to that exception, namely: "But in the case of mere properties, [the rule applies] to the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. Once the twofold nature of the verb has been determined, the discussion of *mantras* is introduced in order to incidentally establish a third mode: their denotative function (*abhidhāyakatva*).

However, the characteristics such as height (tallakṣaṇa) and so forth will be discussed incidentally until the end of the chapter. Then, having stated the distinction [of actions] through synonyms and repetition, an exception to repetition will be made in the section on the Full Moon sacrifice (Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa), because it is a restatement of a composite whole.
Following that, for the purpose of providing exceptions to that [principle], there are the sections concerning the Upāṃśuyāja, the Āghāra, the Agnihotra, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice.
From that point, there is a distinction based on number, name, and quality;
and the investigation concerning qualities continues as far as the section on "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*).
Thereafter, the application of that same principle persists until the section on "different recensions" (*śākhāntara*).

In this regard, the purpose of the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) consists of two things: the exclusion of any cause of difference other than the sixfold [classification], and the removal of doubts concerning name, repetition, quality, and procedure.
This very point must necessarily be stated for the sake of determining the relationship between the primary and the subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgitva*). Not otherwise. (p.
And there is no opportunity for anything else at this point; this is precisely the connection between the chapters.
Why?
Because all [topics], such as the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin), are based upon the differentiation of ritual actions (karmabheda).
When the task is known, there is authority; in the case of an original instruction, there is the cognition of its extension.

First of all, since the inquiry into the meaning of the Veda consists of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no introduction of any other topic such as the definition of difference (*bheda*) at this stage; thus, [the latter] is commenced at a later time.

Even therein, the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣitva*), the relationship of motivator and non-motivator (*prayojaka-aprayojakatva*), and the sequence of performance occur only among distinct acts; therefore, these are not commenced prior to the definition of difference.

Likewise, eligibility (*adhikāra*) can be determined only when the nature of the ritual action (*karma-svarūpa*) has been ascertained, by virtue of its suitability for that action; thus, it awaits all five definitions.

Likewise, because the latter hexad is the subject of extended application (*atideśa*), its accomplishment depends upon the knowledge of the primary instruction (*upadeśa*); thus, as a whole, it depends entirely upon the preceding hexad.
Consequently, this relationship pertaining to the definition of the divisions [of action] is established by elimination (*pariśeṣasiddha*), and it is here that [the section] begins with the words:
"The division of action is sixfold," using the term "division of means" (*sādhanabheda*) as a figurative designation.

The designation [of the sixfold division] should have been recited immediately after the number, in accordance with the sequence of the sūtras to be explained; however, it was recited at the end out of disregard. The particle *iti* has the sense of a reason;
that is to say, the sixfold division of action is [established] by these causes.

Alternatively, having derived the word *bheda* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), the other terms such as *śabdāntara* (differentiation by word) and so forth should be explained through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*) alone.

We shall explain at their proper place how there is no tautology between the term "name" (*saṃjñā*) and "differentiation by word" (*śabdāntara*), nor between "number" (*saṅkhyā*) and "quality" (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, because these always have distinct objects, they do not function like "direct audition" (*śruti*) and the other means of proof.
The intention is merely to demonstrate the distinctions between them, thinking that a consideration of their relative strength and weakness will follow;
other matters are addressed by way of introduction and so forth.
In this context,
they declare that reflection (cintā) for the sake of accomplishing the subject at hand constitutes the introduction (upodghāta);
for what follows from the relevant topic arises through the sequence of the primary and the secondary (prasaktānuprasakta).

Thus, this very section will serve as an introduction for the purpose of establishing the distinction between the various types of *apūrva* that are produced in connection with the subject matter at hand:
from which word, when connected with the fruit, are the distinctions and non-distinctions of the *apūrva* to be understood?
If both the sentence and the meaning of the sentence were partless, then the investigation beginning with "Is dharma [derived] from each word? and so forth would be entirely irrelevant;
therefore, he says: "And the meanings of words reside in the sentence. To this, an objection is raised:
When the meaning of the sentence is established as being characterized by the injunction (codanā), how can it then be doubted that dharma is expressible in every word? (7)

For if the essential nature (svarūpa) of a dharma were being directly expressed, then the inquiry as to what is stated by each individual word would be appropriate; however, since [the meaning] is indicated through secondary implication (lākṣaṇika), such an inquiry is improper.
This is now explained.
The status of being a *dharma* is appropriate for a category of things (*padārtha*) alone because of its connection with the result;
therefore, it is proper to investigate whether this applies to one [category] or to all. (8)
And here, one does not investigate whether every single factor (*dharma*) is expressed by each individual word;
rather, [the question is]:
is that which is expressed by each word a *dharma* that, subsequent to the connection with the result, is understood as having the nature of the sentence-meaning?
Alternatively, it may be that a single category of entity is assisted by the other categories of entities;
in this way, all [categories] are established as being the nature of dharma (*dharmatva*),
because it is accepted that the nature of dharma belongs solely to that which directly accomplishes the fruit.
However, there is no single meaning common to all [words] such that it could be accepted as being one and the same for all.
Furthermore, they consider the meaning of that word which is connected with the word denoting the fruit (*phala*) to be the *dharma* and the means to the *apūrva*.
Therefore, the inquiry is: do all words connect with the fruit, or is it only one?
What is obtained? "At every step.
Why?
The connection is established through uniformity and with the principal element;
therefore, every word is connected precisely with the word denoting the result.
For if a distinction were perceived— namely, that "this is fit for connection with the fruit" and "this is not"— [then there would be a basis for such a classification].
Then, only a small portion would be connected [to the result];
however, when [the connection] is not understood [otherwise], all words are connected with the result itself.
And if even one [word] were connected to the result, [the rest would follow].
It is postulated that the other [elements] are connected with that; however,

according to the principle of the Vājapeya section, since one [element] stands in a subordinate relationship (*guṇabhāva*) by being enjoined as a means toward the result, while the other stands in a predominant relationship as the object of reference (*uddeśa*) and restatement (*anuvāda*), there arises the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by this structural inconsistency (*vairūpya*).
Because all [the constituent acts] being undertaken for the sake of the fruit possess a single form, the occurrence of a *tantra* (common procedure) connection is established.
Furthermore, when possible, everything always connects with the primary element rather than bypassing it in favor of a subordinate one.
Therefore, because all are connected to the fruit, they possess the nature of *dharma*.

In that regard, however, one may conceive as one pleases whether they accomplish the entire fruit individually like the *sattra* sacrifices, or collectively like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and likewise whether it is by way of option (*vikalpa*) or combination (*samuccaya*), and so forth.
In this regard, because the stages of the fruit are more significant,

because there is no employment of the word "one" (eka), and because— as in the case of the three sacrificial fires— the capacity for accomplishment is understood to belong to each individually, the position is that the fruit arises separately from all [the means].
Alternatively, according to the principle of the Varuṇapraghāsas and others, the fruit belongs to those [acts] taken together because they are presented as a single syntactical unit.
Alternatively, because [the word] is satisfied by one [meaning], it is not possible for it to be connected with another at that very moment;
therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*). To this, it is replied:
The *apūrva* is postulated as that which has a connection with the fruit; and when its existence can be established through something less [than that], a manifold postulation is not logical. (10)
For if the sentence were to terminate merely in the connection with the fruit, then perhaps all [the subsidiaries] would be connected with the fruit;
but here, since that much alone is not established, another factor, the *apūrva*, must be postulated.
And that [inference] lacks the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, when a sentence is established by the postulation of a single *apūrva*, there is no grounds for the postulation of another unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
For he who postulates multiple *apūrvas*—

He postulates one [entity]; and if that is what is postulated, then since the sentence has its purpose fulfilled, the presumption of "otherwise-being-impossible" (*anyathānupapatti*) is exhausted and does not serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another *apūrva*.

Therefore, only one [of the two] is connected with the fruit, and from that [connection], the *apūrva* [arises]; the other is determined to be merely an auxiliary that assists that which possesses the fruit.
And there will be no contradiction here,
because the term is resolved as being a name (*nāmadheya*),
or else, by necessity, one resorts to a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the statement: "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*."

Alternatively, since the grasping of their own respective instruments by the verbal roots is established through the medium of the implied portion of the object to be accomplished (*sādhyāṃśa*), this being the case, which one [of the two] should be connected? Thus, when an unrestricted application (*aniyama*) results from avoiding the assumption of multiple unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) in every way, it is said:
The primary act is that which is connected with the fruit; it is held that what is connected to that is a subsidiary.
And it is not possible for a single thing to possess the status of being both a primary act and a subsidiary within the same context. (11)

For it is not logical that within a single sentence the very same thing should sometimes be the primary element due to its connection with a result, and sometimes be a subsidiary element due to its assisting that which possesses the result;
this is because the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal is of a fixed nature.
Therefore, the cognition of the *apūrva* arises necessarily from either a verbal root (*ākhyātapada*) or a nominal stem (*nāmapada*).
But what, then, is *bhāva*?

Which, then, are the words expressing being (*bhāvaśabda*)? They are all the verbal forms (*ākhyātaśabda*) found in sentences connected with results, such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, *juhoti*, and so forth; for in these, the meaning of the suffix is predominant, and the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is produced in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

This is the question of one who considers that there is either an expression of the agent qualified by the sacrifice and so forth, or, conversely, an expression of the sacrifice and so forth qualified by the agent.

Furthermore, even though both questions are established by a single inquiry— since he speaks of the "state of being a verbal root" (*bhāvārthatā*) without even citing the examples "sacrificing" (*yajana*), "the act of sacrificing" (*ijyā*), or "sacrifice" (*yāga*)— [he asks this].
"Therefore, surely there must be some extraordinary words for 'being' (bhāva) as well"—this is the twofold question.

But the proponent of the established view (siddhāntin), having derived the word *bhāva* as a specific term for "productive activity" (*bhāvanā*) by adding the suffix *ac* to the causative form of the root *bhū* according to the rule *er ac*, and intending to show—through positive and negative concomitance—that the verbal suffix denotes that [activity] and excludes the expression of the agent, cites the examples: "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) and "he gives" (*dadāti*).
The opponent, however, [argues]: this meaning is not expressed by anything other than the causative (*ṇijanta*) form of the root *bhū*;
nor does the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*) have an operation here, because it belongs to the meaning of a different root.

Granted that the *dhātus* themselves might denote [the action] by virtue of belonging to the same class [of verbal roots], yet they are incapable of doing so because they are words denoting sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like; thinking this, he says: "But surely the words *yāga*, *dāna*, and *homa*...
To this, it is replied: [The *dhātus* are not the primary denoters, for] it is stated here: "In this regard, it is said."

That which consists of the essence of *bhāvanā* (productive activity), permeated by sacrifice and giving, is understood from verbal roots (*ākhyāta-śabda*) as being eternal; therefore, it is accepted that these [verbal roots] have *bhāva* (action) as their meaning. // 12 //
For whatever meaning is understood from a word that cannot be obtained from anything else—
that is the entire meaning of the word. And in every verbal form, both the meaning of the root and the productive activity (bhāvanā) colored by it are cognized.
Therefore, there is the designation [of verbs] as having "bhāva" (action/state) as their meaning.
However, words denoting substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*), which are understood to be distinct from that [bhāva], were not questioned, as they are already well-known.
Among those, the words for substance and so forth denote already accomplished entities (*niṣpanna-artha*).
Because it is capable of being an instrument, it follows that there is a connection with the result. // 13 //
For in all cases, because it is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the result requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that is already established in form,
not another thing to be accomplished. And since the meaning of the noun is already established, it is capable of fulfilling that requirement.
It is not the meaning of the verbal suffix,
because it is itself that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Therefore, when it is argued that the fruit [is produced] by means of substance (*dravya*) and so forth— [this being the position reached],...
An answer is given by means of a scriptural verse:
"Those words which denote action have the sense of bringing something into being; from them is understood the performance of an apūrva (unprecedented result).
Through them, one should effect heaven by means of sacrifice; for this is the meaning that is enjoined. (14)
The cause for the attainment of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) is the connection with the fruit;
and that connection is preceded by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
And that [expectancy] is observed to proceed from words denoting action (*bhāvaśabda*).

It is not [derived] from words denoting substances or qualities; therefore, from verbal roots (*ākhyāta*), the *apūrva* (the unprecedented) and *bhāvanā* (efficient force) are understood. And therein, the meaning of the verbal root is apprehended as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Because of proximity,
it is determined that the apūrva is brought about by that very [action] which serves as the instrument for the fruit, since otherwise [the production of the fruit] would be impossible.

But how, again, by setting aside the roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and so forth, is the meaning of *bhāvanā* obtained as being expressed solely by the suffix, as in "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*)? Why?
Because: "For the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others would express only the injunction (*vidhi*) by their own power;
by what part, then, could the meaning of the causative form of the root *bhū* (*bhāvaya-*) be expressed? (Verse 15)
Furthermore, sacrifices and the like do not convey the meaning of another verbal root (dhātu), because they are occupied solely with their own respective meanings;
therefore, this [meaning] "one should bring about" (bhāvayet) is merely superimposed upon them, even though it is devoid of any corresponding word.
Furthermore,
even when the meaning of one word is expressed by synonyms, that synonym is not employed together with the original word in reference to that same meaning. (16)
For example, when it is said, "Bring the *pika*," if someone does not understand the meaning of the name, one uses only the word "kokila" for him, rather than saying "the *kokila* is the *pika*."

Likewise, in this context, if the verbal root *karoti* (to do) or the causative *bhāvayati* is a synonym for the verb (*ākhyāta*), then when expressing its meaning, only that [root] alone should be employed, and not even the verbal suffix (*ākhyātapratyaya*).
For at that time, it is not discerned by way of analysis which specific portion conveys the action;

however, in this context, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is indeed employed once again in the forms *bhāvayet* or *kuryāt*. And therefore, that meaning which is conveyed by this [suffix] following the root *yajati* (to sacrifice),...
Since that [root *bhū*] is also [used] by that very same [grammatician] even beyond [the limit of the Vedic roots], the root *bhāvayati* is merely an addition;
therefore, it is non-Vedic. To this, it is replied:
In all cases,
when there is a verbal suffix expressing an accomplished agent and action,
the meaning of "doing" (karoti) is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). // 17 //

In this context, when the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*) is uttered after certain verbal roots (*dhātu*), it expresses an activity (*vyāpāra*) consisting merely in the agent’s acquisition of selfhood;
as in the case of the roots *as*, *bhū*, and *vid*.
But from others, while the agent is already established, [the suffix expresses] another acquisition of selfhood—
The cognition of activity toward an object,
such as "he sacrifices," "he gives," "he reads," or "he goes."

And it is the substance itself— endowed with specific powers, its essential nature set in motion, its own-being dispersed, existing as a sequence of prior and posterior states, fallen from its initial condition and not yet having reached the final state—
that becomes what is denoted by the term "activity" (*vyāpāra*).
In that regard, at times the agent alone is perceived in such a state.
Sometimes, when the agent is already established, there is another [condition]: namely,

when this state belongs to the agent himself, then, because he does not exert effort toward the accomplishment of another while awaiting his own acquisition of selfhood from something else, he does not partake in being denotable by the word "to act" (*karoti*).
But when, having acquired its own nature, it is occupied with something else, then it is designated as "it acts.
And thus, we observe the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in both general and specific forms, such as: "What does he do? He reads; he goes."
But one does not employ [the verb] in the sense of "what does it do? or "does it exist?";
therefore, verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) signify the activity of an agent who has already attained its own nature, and thus possess the meaning of "doing.
And in that case, there must necessarily be something by which [that activity] is being performed.
Why is this?
Because there is no agent of the action of "doing" (karoti) without something being done;
and the agent of the sense of "becoming" (bhavati) becomes the object of the action of "doing. (18)
Since the root *kṛ* is always transitive, as long as that which is being produced (*kriyamāṇa*) is not obtained, the meaning does not reach its final completion.

Furthermore, while all factors of action (*kāraka*) are established as agents (*kartṛ*) with respect to intermediate actions, they become objects (*karman*) and so forth with respect to the primary action.
A distinction arises;
and due to the difference in capacity for each individual action, a variety of intermediate actions occurs.
In this regard, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is understood that the agent of the action [of becoming] becomes the object of the verb "to do" (karoti).
For instance,
that which does not have constant existence, or that which has the state of being eternally existent [cannot be the object].
For that [non-existent thing], there can be no state of being produced, just as in the case of a sky-flower or space. // 19 //

For only that which is already undergoing a process of becoming (*pravṛttabhavana*) or is capable of such a process (*saṃbhāvitabhavana*), when it is engaged by another [agent], is determined as being "in the process of being made" (*kriyamāṇatvena*); nothing else is.
And thus, no one is ever observed making a sky-flower or space.

Even in cases such as "make the feet" (*pādau kuru*), where the application of the action is seen toward things already established, there is no deviation [from the definition], because the words "feet" and so forth are employed with the intention of referring to the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and so on that are not yet fully established.

Furthermore, although the root *kṛ* has multiple meanings, in all instances— such as hinting (*gandhana*), throwing down (*avakṣepaṇa*), and so on— a certain commonality of producing what has not yet arisen is perceived.

Alternatively, since it is observed that at the very moment this [root] expresses the act of bringing into being (*utpādana*), it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a specific finite verb (*ākhyāta*); therefore, it is logical that the object (*karman*) residing therein is precisely that which is being brought into being. By this, the action of "becoming" (*bhavati-kriyā*) is indeed obtained.
And therefore, he who is the agent of the act of doing is the instigator (prayojaka) of the one who is to become;
then, in relation to that [agent], the latter attains the status of the one to be employed (prayojya). (20)

Because of the difference in their capacities, the roots *bhū* and *kṛ* necessarily denote the operations of both the prompted and the prompter, just like the roots *viklid* and *pac*. In that context, sometimes only the operation of the prompter is intended to be expressed— either as one where the operation of the prompted is implied by the expressed capacity for the object (*karman*), or as one where the operation of the prompted is implied by the root itself.
(1) "He makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*) and "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).

(2) Sometimes there is only the activity of the prompted agent (*prayojya*), with the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*) already implied, as in "the jar comes into being" (*ghaṭo bhavati*) or "the rice grains soften" (*viklidyanti taṇḍulāḥ*).
(3) Sometimes both are expressed separately in a combined usage, as in "Devadatta makes a mat" (*karoti kaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*).
And that [action] exists as follows:

sometimes the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) becomes subordinate while the operation of the one being instigated (*prayojya*) is performed, as in the expression "Devadatta acts," or in the usage "he acts by himself."

(5) However, there are occasions when the causal operation (*prayojakavyāpāra*)— in which the action of the instigator (*prayojyakriyā*) has become subordinate by being conveyed through a portion of the same word— is intended to be expressed. In that case, since the roots *kṛ* and *pac* lack the capacity [to denote it] due to their identity [with the action itself],

and since the roots *bhū* and *vi-clid* are restricted solely to the action of the instigated (*prayojyakriyā*) and thus lack the power to directly initiate [the action], the suffix *ṇic* is employed, either as a denoter (*vācaka*) or as an indicator (*dyotaka*), as in *bhāvayati*.
And it is said: "It moistens.
Likewise, he says:
"Those [verbal suffixes] which express the exclusive activity of the prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*)."
Only those [roots] ending in the causative suffix (ṇic) are employed in the sense of the actions of their instigators.
Nor does the fact that those [entities] lack power when they are not in their causal state imply that others must likewise lack power,
nor does the fact that others possess power imply that these too must be so.
Why?
The powers of all entities are not to be questioned regarding their inherent nature;
therefore, bases, suffixes, and so forth, express various meanings.

Thus, by way of the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*), the sense of "bringing about" (*bhāvayati*) is established in all verbal suffixes. Therefore, for a real entity that has attained the status of an agent with respect to its various manifestations (*bhūti*), [the verbal suffix expresses this].
Those who know *bhāvanā* say that *bhāvanā* is the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*). // 23 //
As for the claim that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others do not denote an object distinct from an injunction (*vidhi*),
that is incorrect.
Why?

Grammarians say that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others produce a distinct "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*) of verbal expression; however, a different "productive operation" consisting of the object itself (*arthātmabhāvanā*) is understood from all finite verb endings (*ākhyāta*).

For when the *bhāvanā*—which follows all verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), is denoted by the verbal root *kṛ*, and consists of human effort—is understood, then its specific particulars—such as injunction (*vidhi*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), the past, the future, the present, and so forth—are perceived through specific words distinct from the general term "verbal suffix.
And thus, in every case, the general meaning of "doing" (*karoti*) is understood: "What is he doing? (or "What should be done?")
"He cooks"; what has he done? "He cooked. What will he do? "He will cook. What would he do? "He would cook."
"Should he cook?"—what would he not do?
[The implication is] "he should not cook.

In that regard, within the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose essence is the [human] purpose, there is the instigating activity (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) directed toward the person.

That second [type], the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the denotative function (*abhidhātmikā*) which is a property of the word (*śabdadharmah*), is called "discrimination" (*vibhūti*).

This has been explained in detail in the section on *arthavāda*. As for that which was stated regarding the transgression of the status of synonyms due to the non-abandonment of the suffix, it is replied as follows:
Because the root alone is not employed, because it includes the agent, number, and so forth, and because the preservation of its form is established, the suffix is also employed. (25)
For if the roots *kṛ* (to do) or *bhū* (to become) were alone capable of being employed in usage,
then, just as in the case of the word *pika* when the word *kokila* is used, the suffix would not be employed;
however, there is no employment of a verbal root in isolation.
Because that would result in the undesirable consequence of it being a corrupt form (*apabhraṃśa*).
Therefore, when any suffix whatsoever is to be employed, whichever [word] expresses its meaning is used as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of favoring the base (*prakṛti*), and no other.
Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of [the word] undergoing a change into a different meaning altogether.
But surely, since the suffixes *ik* and *tip* are prescribed for the indication of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the forms *karoti* and *bhāvayati* ought to be used in connection with those [suffixes].
This is not so;
for if that were the case, since the word would have the object as its meaning, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) could not be expressed by those two at all.
As for the fact that in some instances they employ the verbal root even with respect to the object, using forms such as *yajiḥ* or *yajatiḥ*, [this is merely a usage].
It should be understood that when that word is uttered, the cognition of the object occurs through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā);
and there is nothing here [that would prevent this].
There is no purpose in employing that which is non-expressive,
for by doing so, another undesirable consequence would follow, namely, that the verbal roots *kṛñ* and *bhū* would be denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Therefore, they are employed only in conjunction with the verbal suffix in order to establish their orientation toward meaning.
If *bhāvanā* alone were the meaning of the suffix, then either the roots *karoti* or *bhāvayati* would be capable of conveying the entire meaning of the suffix;
in that case, their use by themselves might be suspected [as sufficient].

However, since neither of those two is the case, even though the sense of *bhāvanā* has already been expressed by *karoti* or *bhāvayati*, the suffix is pronounced again in order to convey the agent, number, and so forth.

However, that portion of the meaning which consists of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is restated (*anūdyate*) because it has already been established [by other means]. Otherwise, there would be the misconception that the suffix expresses only the *bhāvanā*, or that both "to do" (*karoti*) and "to bring about" (*bhāvayati*) express the agent, number, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *bhāvanā*, being always characterized by a sequence of prior and posterior stages, is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).

In that case, if another suffix were employed, then [the action], being expressed as having its form condensed like a substance by means of the roots *karoti* and *bhāvayati*, would not be described as resembling a verbal form (*ākhyāta*).
Therefore, the *tiṅ*-suffix must necessarily be employed as well.
Furthermore:
"And when a verbal root is being understood through the proximity of a suffix..."
To whom it should be addressed is never clearly perceived. // 26 //
For if its status as having the meaning of a suffix were determined to be absolute,
then there would arise the suspicion of redundancy regarding the suffix when used with the roots *karoti* and *bhāvayati*;
however, that is not the case.
Because [the meaning] is understood when both are present; for since there is no usage of the base (prakṛti) or the suffix (pratyaya) alone, their distinction cannot be discerned.
Indeed, it can be said that the meaning is expressed by the suffix together with the verbal root (dhātu).
Or rather, [the action is expressed] by the verbal root assisted by the suffix,
or by both;
and there is no difference in the postulation of their respective powers.
This is because, in every respect, they are equal in terms of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Furthermore, there is no purpose for the knowledge of their distinction.
This might be argued:
The claim that *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is understood only from verbal roots ending in *kṛt* suffixes— where it does not deviate from the sense of the *tiṅ* suffix—
is incorrect;
for it is not observed even in the case of suffixes following the roots *as*, *bhū*, and *vid*.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is absolutely no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) even in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes,
because some degree of diminished form is perceived.
First, in the case of *kṛtya* suffixes, such as in "one should eat" (*bhoktavyam*) or "one should sacrifice" (*yaṣṭavyam*), something slightly less than a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is understood.

Even there, because of the primacy of the substance among those things produced by action, the rule "a Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" is weaker than those [prohibitions] produced by abstract states (bhāva); for in that case, there is no primacy of the agent's instigating activity,
since in one instance the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is primary.

In other cases, however, it refers to the prompted agent as qualified by its own operation. By this, the *tiṅ*-suffixes produced in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*) are also explained;
for in those cases as well, the cognition of the subordinate nature of the prompter's operation is no different.
Therefore, there is no equality between finite verbs (*tiṅanta*).

Likewise, although there is no difference in the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) stating that indeclinable gerunds (*avyayakṛt*) denote the abstract state (*bhāva*), the cognition of the mental construction (*bhāvanā*) is self-evidently slightly inferior [to that of finite verbs].
He offers while stepping forward;
he offers by striking with a young blade of darbha grass;
having pressed [the soma] and offered it, they consume it.
In the phrase "before speech was uttered," the *bhāvanā* is understood by the scripture itself as being dependent on another *bhāvanā*; this is evident everywhere.

(3) Even in the case of "cooked" (*pakvaḥ*) or "one who has cooked" (*pakvavān*), the perception of a substance qualified by a *bhāvanā* whose form has been completed is directly perceived. (4) The same should be observed regarding [words] such as "cook" (*pācaka*).
And thus, in all cases, dependence upon a *kāraka* (participant in an action) is observed;

otherwise, this [dependence] would not exist as it does in the case of primary derivatives (*rūḍhi*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*). Furthermore, these designations do not apply to things that are devoid of activity.
And there is no such operation in which something non-existent is not produced;
therefore, the meaning of the roots *karoti* (to do) and *bhāvayati* (to bring into being) is established.

Furthermore, it is possible to demonstrate grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in all cases even without [the action] being constituted by a temporal sequence of prior and posterior stages.
For example: "What is to be done? "It is to be cooked. "In what manner does he offer the oblation?
"Stepping forward."
Having done what does he offer? Having pressed [the juice]. What has he done? He has cooked it. What?
What has been done? It is cooked.
What is Devadatta doing?
"What is this action [denoted by] 'the cooker' (paktā)? It is 'cooking' (pākaḥ).

Furthermore, there exists no means of knowledge for *bhāvanā* in verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) other than its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root "to do" (*karoti*). Therefore, even verbal roots do not abandon *bhāvanā*.
And so they have said: "The root *kṛ* [is used] for the meanings of all verbal roots.

As for its predominance, let that—whether it be denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) or merely indicated (*dyotya*)—be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but not its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

But even so, since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) has been extracted as "by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is also already included by that very same [root]; therefore, the further employment of the word "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*) would not be required.
This is not a fault.
For, when the meaning of a verbal root possessing two meanings is being stated separately, the specific form "by means of sacrifice" is extracted in the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
But the other [aspect], which consists of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and has a general form, is expressed by the phrase "one should bring about [the result] through another word.
Alternatively, it can be said that certain elements— such as the instrument, the agent, and number— are denoted separately by the verbal root and the suffix,
whereas the *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the two combined, because it is never found apart from the aggregate.

Furthermore, both the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya have relied solely upon the grammatical coordination in the statement "words denoting action are those whose meaning is bhāva," rather than stating that the suffixes denote bhāva.
In the Śāstra, however, the conventional usage everywhere is that the meaning of the suffix is bhāvanā.
In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows:
the base and the suffix always express their meanings together for the sake of the suffix.
Because of its predominance, it is by that [suffix] that the meaning of the suffix is determined as *bhāvanā*. // 27 //
Even though there is no other cause for distinction,
nevertheless, by observing that the property of being the meaning of the suffix is predominant, it is understood that "this is certainly the meaning of the suffix.
Likewise, in the case of the two— base and suffix— which always follow a fixed sequence:
At the time of hearing the teaching on conditions, the nature of cultivation is understood. // 28 //
It is not only these two [types of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which are observed through mutual exclusion;

for in that very same word, the distinction is determined by the principle: "When that [element] is present, that [meaning] is seen. As for the claim that even a cognition directed toward "is" (*asti*) and so forth abandons the *bhāvanā*, this applies equally to both the positions regarding the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the collection [of the suffixes].
In every case where something is cognized,
its status as the meaning of the suffix is first determined;
however, in other instances, this very inquiry does not even arise.
Furthermore, an answer to the charge of deviation has been stated in the *Tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*.
Alternatively, there is no deviation here either.
Why?
Even in cases such as "it exists" (*asti*), there is indeed a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the agent as the object to be brought into being;
however, because it is not fully manifested in other respects, it does not appear in that way.

Although, because the agent is not yet fully accomplished and there is no object to be brought into being that is distinct [from the agent], the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is not very clearly perceived in verbs such as *asti* ("to be"),
nevertheless, by the force of the suffix, it is understood that "he brings [himself] into being" (*bhāvayati*).
When the expectation arises as to "what?"— and since nothing else can be conceived while the agent is unaccomplished— it is connected precisely with "himself" (*ātmānam*).
By what? By "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). In what manner?
By the mode of generating parts and so forth.
Thus, all three factors therein are fulfilled by cultivation alone, because no other operation is possible.
In this regard, some components are employed as active in the process of becoming (*bhāvanā*), while others, having their own becoming already established, are the instigators (*prayojaka*).

And the universal (*sāmānya*) that resides within both that which has its becoming established and that which has its becoming unestablished is called "bringing-into-being" (*bhāvanā*) due to its contact with both.

By this, [terms such as] *jāyate* (is born), *niṣpadyate* (is accomplished), and *sidhyati* (is perfected) are explained. Furthermore, the verb *asti* (is), which expresses a state subsequent to the root *bhū* (to become)—which has the same meaning as *jan* (to be born)—receives a verbal suffix in the sense that "being an existence (*sattā*), it brings about its own becoming (*ātmabhavana*).

In that case as well, one must follow the same procedure as before by postulating the operations of the prompted and the prompter, according to the form of general existence characterized by prior and posterior distinctions made by time.
Even though such cultivation (bhāvanā) exists, injunctions and prohibitions are impossible because they have as their object an agent who is a conscious being already established [in existence].
This might be argued:
"An injunction is also observed; therefore, it must belong to the officiating priest (ṛtvij) of the Prāyaṇīya day."
It ought to be so; the Rathantara [Sāman] occurs; here the Adhvaryu priest should be present.
"It might be that there are Ukthya sacrifices here"—
this is true as it appears, but the meaning here is not the same as that of the preceding [passage].

For it is said that a person who is already established [as a priest] should bring about his status as an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)—which is caused by his connection to the ritual action—by means of other activities such as being hired (*parikrayaṇa*).

Likewise, although there is a connection with the root *bhū* (to become) in the case of the *rathaṃtara* and other chants through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), since that is impossible there, it is the inferred efficient force (*bhāvanā*) itself that is enjoined.

However, where the usage "let so-and-so become" (*ihāmuko bhavet*) occurs, because the root *bhū* has the sense of "staying," it is indeed possible for something distinct to be brought about; thus it is understood that something else is to be brought about by means of staying (*sthāna*).

"One should cultivate something" (kiṃcid bhāvayet). By this, the status of "cultivation" (bhāvanātva) belongs only to the non-ultimate activity of the agent (bhavitṛvyāpāra) as expressed through mere references to the past, future, and present,
and not to [the meanings of] injunctions (vidhi) and so forth.

Even when there is a statement regarding [the existence of] past entities and so forth, if the verbal root alone assumes the entire operation (*vyāpāra*) and does not rely on distinctions created by its parts such as time and so forth,

then— due to a clear contradiction— it is merely the meaning of the verbal root that is understood; and the agent, number, and so forth are determined as being the referents of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*), not the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).
And it has already been stated that there is no fault due to the non-deviation of *bhāvanā*.
As for the claim that even in the case of words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*), verbal roots (*dhātu*) do not deviate from *bhāvanā*:
it is true that they do not deviate from the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*).
Furthermore, because it is understood by those very [factors] themselves, it can also be said that it is not denotable;
for it is understood as being subordinate precisely by the factors (kārakas) of the verbal root's meaning.
Therefore, that which consists of the act of cultivation is not at all denoted by words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛt*).

Just as in the case of a verb (ākhyāta), because the action (bhāva) is the primary element, the agent and object are understood merely through their connection to it as subordinate factors— and thus there is no direct denotation of the agent or object— likewise, because the action is established simply through the denotation of the agent and so forth (by the principle of *anyathānupapatti*), there is no direct denotation [of the action]. Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *kṛ* ("to do") occurs precisely in relation to that which is being understood [as the action].

Just as the word *pacati* [is connected] with the word *devadatta*, so too the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*) will be established in that very same manner. Alternatively, since the factors of action exist for the purpose of accomplishing the meaning of the verbal root— which is itself subordinate to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)— the connection with the meaning of the verbal root alone is established.
For it is that very [efficient force] which requires them for its own accomplishment;
and since the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) likewise apprehends them as being of such a nature, the relationship is not contradictory.

As for the verbal suffixes (*kṛtya*), however, because they express an injunction (*praiṣa*), even though they do not directly denote the efficient force, their own meaning is not fully realized until an efficient force complete with its three constituent parts is obtained.
Why?
Because a person is enjoined as an agent with respect to his own activity; and what is the object of that [enjoining] through the commands? It is the *bhāvanā*, which consists of three factors. (31)
For a person is not able to perform anything other than his own activity;
and the injunctions (praiṣas) cause him to perform it.
If those [injunctions] were not to somehow include that activity, [they would be ineffective].
Even on the grounds that they would not be able to be enjoined [to perform the act], the establishment of the implied injunction (*bhāvanākṣepa*) is achieved;

and whatever command (*praiṣa*) pertains to the Brāhmaṇa, all of that, due to the absence of prior acquisition (*prāpti*), becomes a primary injunction (*vidhi*) even without [the need for] traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*).
The capacity to enjoin actions is [the function of the optative suffix].
And this alone is the distinction between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a directive (*praiṣa*):
when [the action] is already established, the recollection of the impulsion is called a directive.
Everything that has not yet attained the status of an injunction acquires the nature of a prescription.
Therefore, it is established that *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the suffix.
Now, if it is maintained that *bhāvanā* is the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), [then...]

Consequently, since activities such as placing [the vessel] on the fire belong to the root *pac* (to cook), and mental resolve belongs to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), these would possess the nature of *bhāvanā*; and since these alone are the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), the *bhāvanā* would be denotable solely by the verbal root.
This is not a fault;
for although this [cognition] is not perceived as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root, it is nevertheless understood through its universal form as something other. // 33 //
For in every case, such as the act of placing [the pot] on the fire and so forth, even the aspect of a general operation (*sāmānyavyāpārāṃśa*) is perceived when one says "he acts.
The operations denoted by verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks)—namely, softening, placing on the fire, and so forth—are located either in the object or in the agent.
Among these, that which is defined as having the nature of motion (*parispanda*) merely through the departure from indifference (*audāsīnyapracyuti*) is *bhāvanā*.
However, those specific features residing in the agent or the object that are capable of coloring that [bhāvanā] enter into its very portions of instrument (*karaṇa*) and procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
If this is so, then it follows that the general meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha-sāmānya*) is the *bhāvanā*.
True; it is a generality by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*).
But not in the form of "cowness" (gotva) and so forth.
How so?
For in the case of sacrifice and other such acts, the universal (sāmānya) that constitutes the instrument is indeed something entirely different.
Furthermore, that which is established as something to be accomplished is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā). // 34 //
For in the case of *bhāvanā*, there are indeed general and particular aspects for each individual person.

Likewise, in the sacrifice (*yāga*) and other acts which serve as its instruments, there exists a generality of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha-sāmānya*) inherent therein, which is required by the instrumental aspect of the *bhāvanā* and is denoted by the term "action" (*karman*).
It is held that sacrifices and the like are called specific instances of productive activity (bhāvanā) because they stand in a relationship of qualification to it,
not by virtue of being its individual manifestations.

In the treatises, however, the words "action" (kriyā) and "object" (karman) are sometimes employed in the sense of the verbal root-meaning, sometimes in the sense of the productive operation (bhāvanā),
and sometimes they are used for both due to their close proximity.
Not by the denotation of its own form.
Why?
Because "the nature of what is called *bhāvanā* in a verb, and likewise the nature of the meaning of the verbal root," [is such that it cannot be expressed by the suffix].
It is never described by others using those very same words, nor by any other terms. (35)
For the word *bhāvanā* denotes that which has a perfected nature, has attained the form of a substance (*sattva*), and is connected with gender and number;
yet it is not denoted as such in a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*),
because it is understood there in a form devoid of gender and number.

In this way, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is also to be understood. Thus, by the very words "he performs" (*karoti*) and "he brings about" (*bhāvayati*), a different kind of meaning is perceived: an *bhāvanā* (productive activity) whose instrument is the act of performing or bringing about. And since such a form does not exist in [verbs] such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), they are not synonyms.

In this regard, one must establish the correspondence with the object (*arthasaṃvāda*) without intending to refer to the distinct cognition of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by the immediately preceding condition (*anantarapratyaya*). Therefore, this application [of the term "cognition"] is based merely on its proximity [to the object], not on an identity of meaning; thus it is established that the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) cannot be denoted by any other word.

But as soon as it is cognized, because of its predominance and because it does not depend on any other requirement, it first requires the element of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), asking: "What should one bring about?

In that regard, as long as there is a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) accompanied by an injunction, the status of being an injunction (*vidhitva*), even though previously cognized, is not yet relied upon.
As long as the cultivation is not complete in its three constituent parts, it is not fit for the performance of the ritual.
Furthermore, from the very commencement of the procedure, this is understood: that this rite must be fulfilled with such parts as it requires to be complete.
Moreover, a person acting with deliberation will not perform an activity devoid of human purpose, even if told to do so a hundred times.

Furthermore, human purpose (puruṣārtha) is not sought by anyone as something falling outside the scope of what is to be accomplished (sādhya), because no other object of accomplishment more highly esteemed than that exists. Therefore,
if in this cultivation (bhāvanā) there were an object of accomplishment that was not a human purpose, [it would not be desired].

Consequently, if persons do not engage [in the action], the causal power of the suffix (*pratyaya*) as an instigator would be sublated. Therefore, even though the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)— due to its proximity through being mentioned in the same word— rushes in to fulfill the requirement of the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) aspect, it is nevertheless rejected because of its incompatibility (*ayogyatva*).
For proximity alone is not the sole cause of a relation;
suitability (*yogyatva*) and other factors are also required. As he will state later: "Whichever [word] has a semantic connection with whichever [object].
Furthermore—

The Vedic revelation has merely stated the relationship between the meaning of the verbal root and the bhāvanā; it has no further function in determining that [relationship] as residing in one specific part [of the two]. (36)

Once the mere relationship has been established and the operation of the scriptural statement has ceased, one must resort to the application of [the injunction] to one of the two parts on the basis of suitability.

If that [application] is displaced from the part to be accomplished (sādhya) by the status of being an injunction—which is conveyed by the same suffix and is more proximate—then [the injunction applies to the means].%p.
Therefore, one must wait for the result, thinking that it will surely be accomplished through another part [of the action].
Furthermore,
the cognition of persons regarding the part to be accomplished (the *sādhya*) is not what impels them to act.
For men always know by themselves alone what ought to be done.
For where human activity is dependent upon scripture, there its proximity or remoteness is taken into account;
however, all persons understand beforehand— prior even to the scripture— that the goals to be accomplished consist of heaven, cattle, sons, villages, and so forth.
And then, when the question "What should one cultivate?
arises, even without the scripture, this much is already understood: that there is some human goal (puruṣārtha).
In that regard, only the specific details are required, as they have not yet been understood.
And even that is not [established] by way of its being the probandum itself;
rather,
it is so by way of being the object of this cultivation.
Consequently, there would be a connection with heaven and the like, even though they are remote,

while the connection with the meaning of the verbal root— though already established— would be disregarded; furthermore, because the injunction would become purposeless, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) would be all the more sublated.
Furthermore,
whatever entity has its status as an agent established in some way,
whether in one's own statement or in the statement of another, that entity becomes the probandum (sādhya). (38)
Moreover, in this context, no connection with the action of "coming into being" (bhavanakriyā) is understood for the meaning of the verbal root and so forth;

rather, for heaven and the like, a connection with "coming into being" is recognized because of their association with the word "desire" (kāma). Why? Because heaven and the like are sought after in this manner: "May heaven be mine," thus they come into being.
Therefore, that [agent] is understood as being dependent on cultivation by way of being something to be employed. // 39 //

Then, since the aspect of the goal— such as heaven and so forth— has been determined, the cultivation (bhāvanā) requires an instrument (karaṇa), [answering the question]: "By what means should one cultivate?"
In that case, since the operation [of the suffix] is dependent upon the treatise (*śāstra*), when one relies upon its proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth:

(1) because the fitness or unfitness [of the object] cannot be known from any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); (2) because there is no contradiction with the injunction (*vidhi*), and thus there is no reason to bypass the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is presented through extreme proximity; (3) ...
And since the cultivation of all results is impossible without some specific meaning of the verbal root, it is understood that [the result is achieved] "by means of sacrifice" (yāgena).
Even though the sacrifice itself is not yet accomplished, nevertheless, having been brought to completion by its own means of accomplishment, it will accomplish [the result].
Furthermore, everything is sometimes accomplished and sometimes unaccomplished;
yet, prior to the commencement of the treatise, accomplishment serves no purpose,
because the completion of the instrument is useful only at the time the result is achieved.
And by virtue of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction in things existing in the three periods of time also being instrumental causes (*sādhana*).

Therefore, sacrifices and the like possess the status of instruments (*karaṇatva*); and since that [instrumentality] occurs through the medium of the unseen potency (*apūrva*), the *apūrva* is understood from those words.

And thus, the meaning of the Sūtra can also be understood in this way: "From those verbal roots such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) and others, which denote an entity (*bhāvārtha*) and have the purpose of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the action (*kriyā*) is to be understood.

But [it may be objected]: by the previously stated logic regarding the relationship between the object and the instrument, the understanding of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) would necessarily follow only from a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) associated with a transitive root.

For indeed, by whichever states [the agent] most desires, that portion [of the action] is restricted; therefore, there would be no verbal root meaning whatsoever that could be intransitive when connected with such [an object]. (40)
Either all verbal roots would incur the status of being transitive,
or else there could be no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) from intransitive roots.
This is not a fault.
Why?
Because in a transitive verb, the object to be reached is indeed distinct from the meaning of the verbal root itself.
And in every case, the basis for the meaning of the suffix is indeed something entirely different.

In the expressions "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*) and "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*), one object is obtained through the completion of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), while the other is the object of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

(1) In that regard, sometimes the very object of the verbal root-meaning itself also assumes the status of being the object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), as in: "He produces rice-gruel by means of cooking" (*pākenaudanaṃ bhāvayati*).

(2) On the other hand, sometimes the productive operation, conjoined with the verbal root-meaning as qualified by its own object, is connected with another object, as in: "He produces his own purpose by going to the village," and "by the cooking of rice-gruel."

And this [result], being understood as merely that which is to be attained subsequent to the meaning of the verbal root—even though it is obscured by the end of the verbal root's meaning—is everywhere determined to be the object of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
And that [result] generally enters into a connection with the word "desiring" (*-kāma*) itself, as in: "one desiring happiness should sit," or "one desiring well-being should lie down."
Even though the roots *ās* ("to sit") and *śī* ("to lie down") are intransitive, the sense of "doing" (*karoti*) expressed by the suffix is determined as their object;
therefore, [the suffixes] *svādi* are prescribed [after them]. Consequently, because the root *kṛ* is always transitive, [it takes an object].

(2) Furthermore, since we observe coreferentiality even with intransitive verbs—as in "What does he do? He sits" (*kiṃ karoti āste*) or "What does he do? He lies down" (*kiṃ karoti śete*)—the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is established as transitive in such cases as well.
Moreover, that which is the object of the sacrifice (*yajati*), because it is worthy of worship, is intended as the deity (*devatā*).
Having abandoned that very status of being an object (karmatva) belonging to the son and others, which is based upon the productive urge (bhāvanā). // 42 //
Therefore, since there is no distinction between transitive and intransitive [verbs] in this regard, the formulation "one should cultivate by means of sitting" is also established as a valid usage.
What, then, is the difference between transitive and intransitive [verbs]?
It is said:
A verbal root is transitive when its meaning directly and invariably possesses an object; it is intransitive when [the connection to an object] occurs through a succession of steps. (43)
For actions such as sitting or lying down are not defined by necessity or immediate succession as being "this" or "that";
therefore, they are designated as "intransitive" (akarmaka).
However, verbs such as *pacati* (he cooks) possess transitivity because they are invariably connected to an object that is either being softened (*viklidyat*) or directly related to it;
there is no difference [in this regard] whether [the object] serves as a qualifier of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

This productive activity, being complete in its two constituent parts [the end and the means], requires the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*), since it is impossible for any instrument (*karaṇa*) to function as such unless it is assisted by a method. Thus, [it asks]: "How should one bring about [the result]? (*kathaṃ bhāvayet*)?

And since that [dharma] lacks the capacity for perception or other means of knowledge to assist in its apprehension, it is accessible solely through scripture; thus, being established in some manner according to proximity— since such [direct means] are impossible— it is postulated through the force of presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*) by way of an entirely unseen assistance, following the authority of scripture, through the instruction of direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and so forth, or through extended application (*atideśa*) based on commonality with injunctions (*codanā*).
Therefore, because it is complete, it is enjoined as being fit for performance;

and from that injunction, by the logic of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the injunction of sacrifices and so forth follows— thus the Sūtra on the Meaning of Verbal Roots (*bhāvārtha-sūtra*) is established.

There are certain words denoting action (karmaśabda)—such as *yāga*, *yajana*, and *ijyā*—which ought to have been cited as examples. Instead, the examples of the *Śyena*, *Ekatrika*, and so forth, established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with those [words], are given because they are easily understood as being dependent (*pāratantrya*), since they are words denoting action that arise subsequent to the injunction regarding the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the sacrifice and the like.
For there could never be even the slightest suspicion that independent [words] denote the act of becoming (*bhāvārtha*).
For sacrifices and the like might, even in their independence, occasionally become objects of doubt regarding their status as *bhāvārtha* (verbs denoting an action) based on inference.
Some *bhāvārtha* terms are not "words for ritual acts" (*karmaśabda*); examples such as *bhāvayet* or *kuryāt* illustrate this.

However, terms such as *bhūti* and the like are not *bhāvārtha* in the sense previously described, because they denote the operation of the person being prompted (*prayojya-vyāpāra*); therefore, they are not examples [of the category under discussion].
In this regard, one might somehow derive the word *bhāva* alone through the grammatical analysis of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), while the other two [words] are not so derived.
Nevertheless, those two are also cited as having the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) insofar as they involve a portion of the activity of the prompted agent.

Alternatively, according to the explanation of the meaning of the second sūtra, since the state of being the purpose of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) exists by virtue of expressing a constituent part [of that operation], they are "terms whose meaning is being" (*bhāvārtha*) even without denoting the entire object.
But how is it that these are not verbal roots denoting action (*karmaśabda*), given that the mere root has been stated to be a verbal root denoting action?
Because a general [root] without specific qualification cannot be performed, it is not a verbal root denoting action.
Therefore, since it is only those verbal roots that express specific actions which are taken to have the status of "karma" (object), this objection is not valid.
For if the words *śyena*, *citrayā*, and *darśapūrṇamāsa* were connected with the results, [the aforementioned difficulty would arise].

Therefore, since the sacrifice lacks the status of being an instrument (karaṇa), it is impossible for the word to function as a name based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it; consequently, by means of well-known usage and other criteria, it must be a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, he says: "This being established in this section," why was this not brought forward in that very place?
Because it lacks a connection with the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Now, why is its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) not brought forward here?
Because it lacks a connection with the definition of a particular (*bheda*).
Therefore, the sequence of priority and posteriority is established by the very fact that the two [words] remain in their respective positions;
nor is this sequence intended to refer to the person seeking the fruit (*arthin*),
because of the difference in grammatical case (*vibhakti*), which results from the absence of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-vibhakti*) that expresses the causal relationship.
Alternatively, "having distinct case-endings" (vivibhaktitva) consists in the connection with a specific nominal suffix (sub-vibhakti) that denotes an already established object.
Therefore, words such as "substance" (dravya) and so forth do not have a connection with a result.
And it has been said:
The relationship between the goal to be accomplished and its means is always based upon *bhāvanā*;
therefore, that [relationship] cannot be established without the cognition of *bhāvanā*. (44)
If it is argued that the meaning is the existence of all [words]. // Jaim_2,1.2 //
First of all, the suffix is not intended to express that which has not been previously expressed;
nor could that [meaning] arise from the verbal root itself, nor equally from the nominal stem following it. (45)
If it were intended that the expression of *bhāvanā* belongs exclusively to the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*), or to the verbal root (*dhātu*) independent of the suffix,
then the position favoring the nominal stem (*nāman*) would be weak; however, in this case, just as the verbal root, when assisted by its connection with the suffix, [expresses] *bhāvanā*—
Just as the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) occurs for the sake of producing delight (*nurañjana*),
so it is also for the noun (*nāmapada*); thus, there is no distinction.

Those [factors] whose form is perceived when they arise in their own application are "names" (nāman); therefore, there is no expectation of anything beyond them, because they have already become manifest in their own application. (Jaimini 2.1.3)

Regarding what was said—that when the unseen potency (*apūrva*) arises from one [action], the other will be for its sake—he first demonstrates the distinction residing therein by means of the nature of things.
How so?
"For a property is not desired at every step because it would entail the assumption of many unseen potencies."
There is no refutation of that [objection] regarding the connection of the name with its fruit. // 46 //

If, when one [act] is postulated as having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*), another is understood to serve that same purpose by virtue of its visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), then parsimony (*lāghava*) is attained.
But if, for the sake of establishing that same purpose, yet another unseen factor must be postulated even beyond that, then it is better that all [acts] be connected directly with the fruit itself;
thus, one need not resort to the troublesome burden of heterogeneous relationships (*saṃbandhavairūpya*).
Furthermore, if there is a connection between the name and the result, one must necessarily admit that the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) exists for the sake of assisting it;
and since that [meaning of the root] is something to be accomplished, it cannot provide visible assistance to the meaning of the noun, which is already established in its own nature,
for the meaning of the noun does not depend upon it.
Because it is understood as being already accomplished at the very moment of the employment of the word,
or because that which is to be depended upon is unfit [as an object] due to its being already established;
furthermore, "employment" (*prayoga*)— in the sense of "that in which something is employed"— refers precisely to the denotatum itself.
For the perception of a completed form has that very [action] as its basis.
While it should have been stated that the nature of action is unproduced, the demonstration of its perishability is made even with respect to that which is completed.

Because momentariness entails the necessity of repeated production, there is no further expectation (*parākāṅkṣā*)—meaning no expectation for another [cause]—or no expectation for a primary [cause] in terms of being produced; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Alternatively, the meaning is that "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣā*) is far removed (*parā*) from them.
Why?

Because it is "existent" (*bhūtatvāt*). This was introduced for the purpose of stating its essential nature (*svarūpa*), meaning precisely because it is already accomplished (*niṣpannatvāt*); thus, at the end, the author of the Sūtras taught that very same point as the reason.

However, those verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) whose application is not observed with respect to their own object in the sense of origination—therefore, from them [the action] should be understood, because the application [of the word] is dependent [upon something else]. (Jaimini 2.1.4)
The meaning of a verbal root, residing in a verb, is understood as having the nature of something to be accomplished;
however, when that [accomplished state] is desired as possessing a result, it is accepted that the name (noun) has a perceptible purpose.

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is, by its very nature, something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Specifically, when that which is expressed by the verbal root contained within a verb (*ākhyāta*) is enjoined as a means to an end (*phala-sādhanatva*), then— because it is as yet unestablished (*asiddha-rūpa*) and thus possesses a requirement for a means (*sādhana-ākāṅkṣā*)— the nominal word (*nāmapada*) functions either as an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or as a name (*nāmadheya*).
In either case, its status as being for that purpose (tādarthya) is established solely by what is observed.

[Objection: But in the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), the word denoting the name will also have a goal to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*), and thus it would be equivalent to a verbal root (*dhātu*). [Reply: No;
because when it is connected with a result, it is established as having an already-accomplished meaning (*siddha-artha*) by virtue of being an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Moreover,
when even the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha), which consists of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya), is denoted by a noun (nāman);
Then it is perceived as having a fully established nature, just like a substance. // 48 //
Although the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by way of its actual ontological nature (*vastusvarūpa*),
nevertheless, when expressed by a nominal word (*nāmapada*), it is denoted as having an established form (*siddharūpa*) because it is associated with gender and number.
And the arising of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is caused by the mode of expression, not by the ontological reality itself.
Therefore, it is logical that the expectancy belongs to the verbal root alone, and not to the nominal stem;
furthermore, this is because the actual usage depends upon the root.
Now, the distinction created by the proximity of the word is being stated.

For when *bhāvanā* consists of human activity, even the connection with the meaning of the verbal root is undertaken by the person; and because there is no reason to overstep that [connection], there is no mention of the nominal word (*nāmapada*).
Therefore, there is a distinction.
